slidelink.displaytext: Module 5.4: Practical Application of the 5-Step CQI Process
What You Will Learn in Brief Application 4
Barrier 1: Staff Shortages – How They Affect CQI
Staff Shortages: Cross-Training and Continuity in Practice
Barrier 2: Lack of Buy-In – How It Affects CQI
Strategies to Address Lack of Buy-In
Barrier 3: Time Constraints – How They Affect CQI
Time Constraints: Putting Strategies into Practice
When Barriers Feel Insurmountable: Seeking Technical Assistance

slidetranscripts.slidetranscript:
<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style FlowDirection="LeftToRight" TrailingMargin="0"> <ListStyle ListType="None" ListTypeFormat="Parentheses" BulletFont="Arial" /> </Style> <Span Text="Welcome to Module 5.4, the third installment in the last module of the CQI training series. In this module, we will cover the practical applications of the 5-step CQI process.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Select “Next” to begin." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="As a reminder, by the end of Module 5 you will be able to apply California’s 5-Step CQI Process to prevention services, learn practical steps to integrate the 5-Step CQI Process into agency workflows, and develop strategies to overcome common CQI implementation barriers. This brief application focuses on that last objective: the barriers, and how to respond to them." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Module 5 is divided into four brief applications:
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Brief Application 1: Review of modules 1-4 and how to interpret fidelity and outcome metrics.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Brief Application 2: How to identify and define a problem from fidelity and outcome metrics and how to conduct a root cause analysis.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Brief Application 3: Developing, implementing, testing, and revising solutions.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Brief Application 4: Key implementation barriers and how to address them.In this session, we will be covering Brief Application 4." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Before we dive in, let's preview what you'll be able to do by the end of this module.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="By the end of this eLearning, you'll be able to identify the three most common CQI barriers and explain how each one affects the CQI cycle. You'll be able to describe at least two strategies for each barrier. You'll also understand the specific role of a CQI champion in building organizational buy-in. In the last module we discussed when to seek TA for the evaluation and revision process. In this module we will cover when to see technical assistance with CQI barriers." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Let's start with a high-level overview.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="There are three CQI barriers this module focuses on. The first is staff shortages — when the team doesn't have enough capacity to complete each part of the CQI cycle, or when staff turnover disrupts continuity.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="The second is lack of buy-in — when staff don't see CQI as relevant or meaningful, or actively resist participating.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="And the third is time constraints — when the demands on staff make CQI tasks feel like one more thing on an already full plate.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="One thing to keep in mind throughout this module: these barriers are normal. The goal is not to eliminate them — it's to have strategies ready so that when they arise, the team can respond effectively rather than stalling. We'll cover each barrier in depth, starting with staff shortages." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Staff shortages are one of the most common CQI barriers, and they affect the process in multiple ways.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="The most direct effect is reduced capacity. When there aren't enough people, every step of the CQI cycle takes longer — it takes longer to identify problems, root cause analysis and coming up with a solution is rushed rushed, implementation is inconsistent, and evaluation may get skipped. Competing priorities make this worse. When caseworkers and program staff are focused on serving clients — which is their primary job — CQI can feel secondary, even when it isn't. High turnover adds another layer. When a key team member leaves, they often take institutional knowledge with them — knowledge about the problem, the process, what's been tried before, and what worked. Without documentation and cross-training, that knowledge disappears.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="The important thing to understand is that staff shortages don't just slow the process down — they affect the quality of every step, because each stage in the CQI cycle builds on the one before it." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="There are five strategies for addressing staff shortages in CQI.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="First: cross-train staff on CQI duties. If more than one person knows how to pull the data report, or facilitate the root cause discussion, the team is protected when someone leaves or is out.Second: maintain regular team updates. When all CQI team members brief their colleagues and supervisors consistently, knowledge is distributed — not siloed with one person.Third: automate data collection and reporting wherever feasible. This reduces the manual burden on staff and frees time for higher-value work.Fourth: simplify the CQI process. The more manageable each step is, the more resilient the process is to staffing constraints. This is another reason to choose solutions in the Goldilocks zone.Fifth: be transparent about shortages. Staff are more likely to engage when leadership acknowledges real constraints and is honest about what's achievable. Transparency builds trust." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Let's go deeper on two of the most important strategies: cross-training and continuity planning.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Cross-Training means deliberately identifying the two or three most critical CQI tasks and making sure at least two people can perform each one. It also means documenting the procedures — not just knowing them — so that anyone stepping in can follow the process reliably.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Continuity Planning goes hand in hand with cross-training. It means keeping a shared, up-to-date log of CQI status so the whole team knows where things stand. It means storing data and notes in a shared location — not on personal drives — so information survives any individual departure. And when someone does leave, it means scheduling a structured handoff so their knowledge is captured before they go.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="These practices take time upfront. But they prevent the kind of disruption that stops a CQI cycle in its tracks — and that's a far bigger time cost than the preparation." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="The second barrier is lack of buy-in — and it's one of the most damaging because it undermines the process from the inside.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="When staff don't believe CQI is meaningful, they comply at a surface level but don't engage. Data gets collected but not seriously reviewed. Solutions get designed but aren't implemented with fidelity. Evaluation happens on paper but the findings don't actually change anything.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Three things tend to drive lack of buy-in. Staff may see CQI as irrelevant — disconnected from what they actually do with clients. They may see it as punitive — as if the data review exists to catch them doing something wrong. Or they may simply have too many competing demands and CQI falls to the bottom of the priority list.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="None of these perceptions are irrational. They're understandable responses to real pressures. The strategies for addressing buy-in have to meet staff where they are." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="There are three main strategies for building buy-in.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="First: leadership engagement is essential. Leaders need to explicitly and visibly connect CQI work to what staff care about — the outcomes for families, the quality of services, the team's own goals. When leaders treat CQI as a real priority rather than a compliance exercise, staff take their cue from that.Second: designate a CQI champion. This is a specific role — a non-supervisory staff member who takes on CQI leadership from within the team. The champion builds peer engagement, helps reframe the work in terms colleagues can relate to, and bridges the gap between frontline staff and CQI leadership.Third: celebrate small successes. Progress in CQI is often incremental — a two percent improvement in a screening rate might not feel like cause for celebration. But acknowledging progress, however modest, signals that the work is making a difference and keeps momentum going.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="These three strategies work best in combination. A champion without leadership support is isolated. Celebrations without genuine progress ring hollow." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="The third barrier is time constraints — and it's one of the most persistent because it reflects real demands on staff who are already stretched thin and are practically a given in child welfare settings and/or social service agencies.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Time constraints create resentment when CQI feels like one more obligation on top of everything else. They reduce the organization's ability to complete each part of the cycle thoroughly. And they lead to rushed work — which is particularly dangerous in CQI because of the cascade effect.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="The Cascade Effect works like this: a rushed problem statement leads to a shallow root cause analysis. A shallow root cause analysis leads to a solution that doesn't quite fit. Incomplete implementation produces uninformative evaluation data. Poor quality at any single step ripples forward through every stage that follows.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="This is why time pressure in CQI isn't just inconvenient — it's a genuine threat to the quality and integrity of the whole process." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="There are four strategies for managing time constraints.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="First: design solutions that are realistic given real-world time constraints. If the team doesn't have time to implement a multi-component intervention, don't choose one. This is another argument for the Goldilocks zone — simpler solutions are more sustainable.Second: keep CQI meetings short and focused. Use short, structured routines. Set a clear end time and stick to it. A ten-minute data check-in that happens consistently is more valuable than a two-hour meeting that happens irregularly.Third: integrate CQI activities into existing workflows. If there's already a monthly all-staff meeting, add a five-minute CQI update rather than scheduling a separate meeting. Look for existing structures the team can build on.Fourth: plan ahead for intensive periods. If the team knows that implementation will be demanding in February, reserve dedicated calendar time in December — before the crunch hits. Reactive scheduling is always harder than proactive scheduling." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Let's make these strategies concrete with examples from a home visiting agency.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="A ten-minute data check-in might look like this: at the start of each weekly team meeting, the CQI lead shares one updated data point and asks, "Is this better, worse, or the same as last month?" No formal presentation, no lengthy discussion — just a consistent, brief pulse-check.Integrating into existing meetings, for example, the monthly all-staff meeting — which already happens — gets a standing five-minute CQI update added to the agenda.Planning ahead for implementation crunch means that in December, the team identifies that February will be intensive and blocks CQI sessions on the calendar then — not in January when February is already looming.And choosing a single, simple solution — like the skills workshop rather than the multi-component intervention — is itself a time management strategy. Manageable solutions can be implemented well; complex ones often can't." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Here's a summary of all three barriers side by side.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Staff shortages reduce capacity, threaten continuity, and make every step harder. Key responses: cross-train, document, automate, and be transparent.Lack of buy-in lowers engagement and makes it likely that CQI activities will be done in form but not in spirit. Key responses: CQI champion, link to staff values, celebrate progress.Time constraints rush the work and create the cascade effect — poor quality at one step undermines all the steps that follow. Key responses: simple solution that is easier to implement, structured brief meetings, integration into existing workflows, and planning ahead.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Remember: barriers are normal. The goal is not to have a barrier-free CQI process — that doesn't exist. The goal is to recognize barriers when they appear and respond with targeted strategies rather than letting them stall the work." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Before we close, let's revisit technical assistance — because it applies to barriers as well as to the solution testing process in Module 3.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Sometimes internal strategies aren't enough. A team can cross-train, designate a champion, and restructure its meetings — and still find that barriers are too deep to address from the inside. That's when external support becomes essential.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Consider seeking TA when the team isn’t sure which barrier is driving the problem, barriers persist despite implementing strategies faithfully, or when staff morale or turnover are both so bad that the process can't move forward.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="The phrase worth repeating is: CQI is not a solo activity. The process is designed to be collaborative. Don't wait until things are at a crisis point. Reaching out earlier, when problems are still manageable, produces better outcomes than waiting until they become overwhelming." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Let's close with the key takeaways from this module.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Clearly identify the problem and the root cause: Take your time to interpret the data to correctly understand if a problem is occurring. Problem statements are useful because they help define the scope and extent of the problem. Taking the time to do a root cause analysis helps insure the team chooses a solution that can address the underlying cause of the problem.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Reasonable solutions: As a reminder solutions should fall in the Goldilocks zone- not too simple and not too complicated.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Implementation Planning: Implementation is a complex process! A plan with a measurable aim, baseline, implementation details perhaps including a schedule, and a data and learning plan help insure each stage is clear to the whole team and nothing is forgotten or rushed.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Barriers are normal: Staff shortages, lack of buy-in, and time constraints are common particularly in child welfare and social service settings. Respond with targeted strategies rather than abandoning the process.And seek TA when needed. CQI is collaborative — external support is not a failure." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>

<Document xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"> <Content> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Congratulations — you've completed Brief Application 4.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="You've now worked through all five steps of the CQI process: defining the problem, understanding root causes, identifying and planning a solution, implementing it, testing whether it's working, and navigating the barriers that arise along the way.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="This is the work of Continuous Quality Improvement. It's iterative, it's collaborative, and it's never truly finished — each cycle produces learning that informs the next one.
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="
" /> </Block> <Block> <Style /> <Span Text="Thank you for your time and engagement throughout this training." /> </Block> </Content> </Document>
